items.explanation: James II created the Dominion after Massachusetts defied the Navigation Acts, placing New England under the iron rule of Sir Edmund Andros, who revoked charters and levied taxes without an assembly.
options: A. Increased democracy in the colonies
B. Strengthened the governor's authority in the region
C. Let New England colonies air common grievances
D. Placed the king in direct control of New England affairs
items.stem: The creation of the Dominion of New England

option_explanations.A: The Dominion did not increase democracy. Sir Edmund Andros revoked colonial charters, abolished elected assemblies, and taxed without representation — the opposite of more democracy.
option_explanations.B: The Dominion did not merely strengthen a governor's existing authority: it wiped out the colonies' charters and assemblies and installed a new royal administration over all of New England, so this understates what happened.
option_explanations.C: The Dominion gave the colonies no forum for grievances. With assemblies abolished and dissent suppressed under Andros, New Englanders had no official way to air complaints.
option_explanations.D: Correct. James II created the Dominion of New England after Massachusetts defied the Navigation Acts, placing the region under direct royal control through his governor, Sir Edmund Andros.

items.explanation: The 1739 uprising near Charleston terrified planters, who answered with slave codes and harsher discipline meant to deter further revolts.
options: A. A rise in slave imports to the Southern colonies
B. New fortifications around southern cities
C. Efforts to humanize the Middle Passage
D. Harsher treatment of enslaved people across the South
items.stem: A major consequence of the Stono Rebellion was

option_explanations.A: Slave imports did not rise as a result: frightened South Carolina planters did the opposite, imposing a prohibitive duty that cut slave imports for roughly a decade.
option_explanations.B: Building fortifications was not the planters' response. Their answer to the rebellion was tighter control of the enslaved population, not military construction projects.
option_explanations.C: Nothing about the Middle Passage was humanized after Stono. The rebellion produced harsher slave codes, not kinder treatment of captives in transit.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 1739 Stono Rebellion near Charleston terrified planters, who answered with harsher discipline — South Carolina's 1740 slave code tightened control over every aspect of enslaved people's lives to deter further revolts.

items.explanation: The assemblies alarmed London precisely because they were controlled by colonial elites holding the power of the purse, defying royal instructions and neutering royal governors. They were not democratic bodies — that is the exception.
options: A. Assemblies holding the 'power of the purse' could erode British control
B. Assemblies spread democratic rule through the colonies
C. Assemblies sometimes defied instructions from London
D. Royal governors could barely restrain the assemblies
items.stem: The growth of colonial assemblies worried Britain for all of the following reasons EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: This was a real worry for London: by controlling taxation and spending, colonial assemblies could starve royal governors of funds and thereby erode British control.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. Colonial assemblies were not democratic bodies; they were controlled by local elites. What alarmed Britain was elite assemblies using the power of the purse and defying royal orders, not democracy spreading.
option_explanations.C: This was a real worry: assemblies regularly ignored or defied instructions from London, asserting their own authority against the crown's.
option_explanations.D: This was a real worry: royal governors found they could barely restrain assemblies that controlled the colony's money and claimed the rights of Englishmen.

items.explanation: Under mercantilism the colonies existed to enrich the mother country with raw materials and cash crops — tobacco, rice, indigo, lumber — while buying finished English manufactures.
options: A. To make manufactured goods England preferred not to produce
B. To grow staple crops such as tobacco
C. To supply raw materials such as lumber
D. Both B and C
items.stem: In Britain's eyes, the chief economic function of the American colonies was

option_explanations.A: Britain did not want the colonies making manufactured goods. Mercantilist policy reserved manufacturing for England and actively discouraged colonial industry, so the colonies would buy English finished goods.
option_explanations.B: This was true — tobacco, rice, and indigo were exactly the staple crops Britain wanted — but it is only half the answer, since raw materials mattered just as much.
option_explanations.C: This was true — lumber, naval stores, and furs were exactly the raw materials Britain wanted — but it is only half the answer, since staple crops mattered just as much.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Under mercantilism the colonies existed to enrich the mother country by supplying both staple crops (B) and raw materials (C), while buying finished English manufactures in return.

items.explanation: As the plantation system matured in the 1730s, enslaved laborers were increasingly concentrated on large plantations rather than scattered on small farms, a shift made possible by the booming slave trade after the Dutch lost their monopoly in 1682.
options: A. The Dutch lost their slave-trade monopoly, flooding the colonies with captives
B. Conditions on the Middle Passage grew noticeably milder
C. Enslaved people increasingly lived and worked on large plantations
D. Slave revolts led planters to ease working conditions
items.stem: What change in the southern colonies' slave system began in the 1730s?

option_explanations.A: The slave-trade monopoly had ended decades before the 1730s; the trade was already booming. The 1730s change was in how enslaved people lived and worked, not in who carried them across the Atlantic.
option_explanations.B: Conditions on the Middle Passage did not grow milder in the 1730s. The voyage remained brutally overcrowded and deadly throughout the slave-trade era.
option_explanations.C: Correct. As the plantation system matured in the 1730s, enslaved laborers were increasingly concentrated on large plantations rather than scattered across small farms — the shift the question describes.
option_explanations.D: Slave revolts did not lead planters to ease conditions; uprisings like Stono (1739) produced harsher slave codes and tighter discipline, not better treatment.

items.explanation: The shipping monopoly funneled the carrying trade -- and its profits -- to English merchants and shipyards, deliberately squeezing out the Dutch, who then dominated world shipping. Colonial consumers paid more rather than less, and colonial manufacturing was discouraged, not encouraged.
options: A. Open colonial ports to the ships of all nations
B. Enrich English merchants and shipbuilders by excluding Dutch competitors
C. Lower the prices colonial consumers paid for imported goods
D. Encourage manufacturing industries within the colonies
items.stem: The act's requirement that colonial goods be carried only in English ships was intended to
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the increase of shipping and encouragement of the navigation of this nation, wherein, under the good providence and protection of God, the wealth, safety, and strength of this kingdom is so much concerned... no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands... belonging to his Majesty... but in such ships as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England..."
—Navigation Act of 1660 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The act did the opposite: it closed colonial ports to foreign ships, permitting trade only in English vessels — open ports to all nations is exactly what the law forbade.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The shipping monopoly funneled the carrying trade and its profits to English merchants and shipbuilders, deliberately squeezing out the Dutch, who then dominated world shipping.
option_explanations.C: Colonial consumers did not pay less. Forcing goods through English ships and ports raised freight costs, which colonists paid in higher prices.
option_explanations.D: The act did not encourage colonial manufacturing. Mercantilist policy discouraged colonial industry so that colonists would keep buying English finished goods.

items.explanation: By forcing colonial trade through English ships and ports -- and taxing enumerated goods -- the acts raised costs and bred evasion: smuggling flourished (John Hancock's fortune came from it), and each enforcement effort deepened colonial anger at imperial control.
options: A. The rapid industrialization of the New England economy
B. The abolition of the transatlantic slave trade
C. Widespread smuggling and growing resentment of imperial trade regulation
D. Colonial satisfaction with Parliament's economic stewardship
items.stem: The Navigation Acts contributed most directly to which development in the colonies?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the increase of shipping and encouragement of the navigation of this nation, wherein, under the good providence and protection of God, the wealth, safety, and strength of this kingdom is so much concerned... no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands... belonging to his Majesty... but in such ships as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England..."
—Navigation Act of 1660 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The New England economy did not rapidly industrialize under the Navigation Acts. Its growth came from shipbuilding, fishing, and carrying trade — commerce, not industry.
option_explanations.B: The Navigation Acts had nothing to do with the slave trade's abolition, which came decades later (Britain 1807, the United States 1808) for entirely different reasons.
option_explanations.C: Correct. By forcing colonial trade through English ships and taxing enumerated goods, the acts raised costs and bred evasion: smuggling flourished and each enforcement effort deepened colonial anger at imperial control.
option_explanations.D: Colonists were not satisfied with Parliament's economic stewardship. The acts' restrictions and costs were a major and growing source of resentment toward imperial trade regulation.

items.explanation: Both England and Spain ran closed mercantilist empires: colonies could trade legally only with the mother country's ships and ports, concentrating profits at home. The Dutch practiced relatively open trade, the Corn Law repeal moved Britain toward free trade, and the Embargo was a temporary diplomatic weapon, not a standing imperial system.
options: A. Spain's restriction of colonial trade to Spanish ships and ports
B. The Dutch Republic's open-port trading policy in the seventeenth century
C. Britain's repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846
D. The American Embargo Act of 1807
items.stem: The Navigation Acts most closely resembled which other imperial trade system?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the increase of shipping and encouragement of the navigation of this nation, wherein, under the good providence and protection of God, the wealth, safety, and strength of this kingdom is so much concerned... no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands... belonging to his Majesty... but in such ships as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England..."
—Navigation Act of 1660 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Like England, Spain ran a closed mercantilist empire: its colonies could trade legally only with Spanish ships and ports, concentrating the profits at home — the same closed system as the Navigation Acts.
option_explanations.B: The Dutch practiced relatively open, free-trade shipping in the seventeenth century — the opposite of a closed imperial monopoly, and precisely the competition the Navigation Acts targeted.
option_explanations.C: Repealing the Corn Laws in 1846 moved Britain toward free trade — the reverse of the Navigation Acts, which were protectionist restrictions on trade.
option_explanations.D: The Embargo Act of 1807 was a temporary diplomatic weapon Jefferson used against Britain and France, not a standing imperial trade system like the Navigation Acts.
